The Seagull is BYD’s most affordable electric vehicle, starting at about $10,000 in China and sold overseas as the Dolphin Surf. BYD is preparing to introduce a new version that will likely be an even “bigger” hit.
BYD opens pre-orders for the new Seagull EV
BYD is best-known for its ultra-low-cost vehicles, but the Seagull is much cheaper than anything sold in the US.
In China, BYD’s electric hatch starts at 69,900 yuan, or around $10,000. Meanwhile, the lowest-priced vehicle in the US is the 2026 Hyundai Venue, which costs just over $20,000.
Even in markets outside China, like Europe, the Dolphin Surf, as sold, starts at just €22,900 ($25,000). In places like Brazil and Mexico, the electric hatch is rebadged and sold as the Dolphin Mini.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
As one of the most affordable electric cars in many markets, the Seagull (Dolphin Surf/ Mini) has been among the world’s best-selling EVs.
According to the most recent data from CleanTechnica , BYD’s entry-level EV was the world’s sixth-best-selling EV through August, with over 212,000 units sold. It ranks behind only BYD’s own Yuan Up (Atto2), the Tesla Model 3, Geely Xingyuan (EX2), BYD Song (Seal U), and the Tesla Model Y.
For its second generation, BYD is upgrading the Seagull to compete with the incoming wave of entry-level electric cars hitting the market.
The new Seagull is bigger, smarter, and adds a bit more luxury over its predecessor. We caught a glimpse of the second-gen Seagull last month when Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD’s Ocean series, revealed the first official images .
BYD said shortly after that part of “Growing Up” means living up to expectations. As such, the new Seagull adds premium features, such as ambient lighting and massaging front seats.
It will also offer more legroom for rear passengers and a refined, immersive cockpit design. The setup includes a larger infotainment display, a new two-spoke steering wheel, and a redesigned center console for extra storage.
From what was shown, the new Seagull will not include a traditional instrument cluster behind the steering wheel.
Instead, it will display the information on the center infotainment screen. It also gains physical buttons below the infotainment and on the steering wheel.
BYD opens blind pre-orders for the second-generation Seagull (Source: Zhang Zhou/ BYD)
Zhang announced on Weibo that blind pre-orders for the second-generation Seagull officially opened on Friday with six exterior color options.
However, he didn’t reveal prices, which is common in China when opening blind pre-orders for a new vehicle.
BYD hasn’t confirmed battery specs or any other details. Zhang said during the Chengdu Auto Show in August that the second-generation Seagull will launch as the “Great Seagull,” confirming it will go on sale by the end of 2026.
After the new model appeared in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) regulatory filing in August, we learned a few key details.
For one, the new Seagull is 4,205 mm long, 1,810 mm wide, and 1,570 mm high, with a 2,650 mm wheelbase. That’s 425 mm longer and 150 mm longer in wheelbase than the current Seagull, which measures 3,780 mm in length.
The filing also revealed it will gain a more powerful 95 kW (127 hp) electric motor, up from the 55 kW (75 hp) the current Seagull offers.
Instead of a front-mounted motor like the current Seagull, the new model will switch to a rear-mounted electric motor.
Like many of its new vehicles, the second-generation Seagull now has a roof-mounted LiDAR. As such, it’s expected to offer an upgraded ADAS system with BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system.
We will learn more details soon, with an official launch expected by the end of 2026. While not yet confirmed, the new Seagull is expected to offer BYD’s latest Blade Batteries 2.0 and Flash Charging tech on more premium trims.
After its launch in China, BYD is expected to introduce a larger version overseas, likely as a variant of the Dolphin Surf and Dolphin Mini.
Source: Autohome, BYD

Korean defense contractor Hanwha made its presence known at the show with a few vehicles on display at DSEI 2023, including its new K9A2 self-propelled howitzer. (Lee Ferran / Breaking Defense)
WASHINGTON — Weeks after the Army tapped Hanwha Defense USA for its w heeled self-propelled howitzer modernization program, the company now plans to enter t he service’s new competition for a tracked variant.
“I think it’s a must. I mean, when we had early conversations with the Army, we actually thought the Army might be procuring tracked [variants] first,” Mike Smith, Hanwha USA’s COO and president of Land Systems, told reporters Tuesday.
Hanwha USA is looking at a “menu of options” for the competition — namely either its K9A1 or K9A2 tracked vehicles, Smith said. While he noted that the K9A1 is widely available and the “most cost-effective” option, the newer K9A2 variant features more modern capabilities.
According to Hanwha’s website , the K9A1 variant has a 155mm and 52-caliber ca nnon with a range of over 40 kilometers. At full capacity, it can fire six to eight rounds per minute for three minutes.
The K9A 2 is the company’s newer tracked variant. The howitzer has the same drive power as the K9A1, but features a fully automated turret capable of firing nine to 10 rounds per minute. The K9A2 also has two “independent” loading arms for projectiles and propellants, as well as a new autoloader system to increase the rate of fire and reduce the number of crew members needed.
The service recently awarded Hanwha $233 million for the accelerated delivery of six wheeled prototype howitzers, with an option for an additional 12. Both new wheeled and tracked variants are intended to replace the Army’s towed M777 and self-propelled M109A7s howitzers, the latter of which was originally fielded in the 1960s.
Smith’s comments come after the Army’s Program Acquisition Executive for Fires posted a request for information (RFI) on Sept. 30 seeking tracked howitzers and a coinciding resupply vehicle. The solicitation asked vendors for potential production lead times, maximum production capability , strategies to on shore US production if the vendor’s facilities are abroad and more.
Smith said the company currently has several variants of both vehicles being sold to other land forces, which could make the production lead time for the Army shorter if the service selects one of Hanwha’s tracked variants. However, he didn’t reveal what that lead time would look like.
The howitzers are “completely tailorable,” he added, meaning the company can make small tweaks to its vehicles if needed in order to meet the Army’s formal requirements.
A spokesperson from PAE Fir es told Breaking Defense earlier this month that the Army is pursuing separate tracked and wheeled howitzers because the two variants “ address different operational requirements and formations.”
The spokesperson said the wheeled variant is intended to provide more mobility, survivability and “responsiveness” for formations with towed artillery, while the tracked variant is better suited “for employment” with armored formations.
Traditionally, wheeled vehicles are also lighte r and best suited to driving on roa d s. Tracked vehicles often feature heavier chassis that can more easily maneuver in muddy or rougher environmental conditions.

Volkswagen unveiled the ID. Tiguan, an all-electric version of its best-selling vehicle. The ID. Tiguan will go on sale in early 2027, replacing the ID.4 and ID.5 with up to 372 miles of range and plenty of other upgrades.
Meet the ID.4’s replacement, the Volkswagen ID. Tiguan
The ID.4 and ID.5 are on the way out as the new ID. Tiguan steps in. With over 950,000 models sold since they went on sale in 2021, the ID.4 and ID.5 have been at the core of Volkswagen’s EV lineup.
Following the ID. Polo and ID. Cross, the ID. Tiguan is the next to go on sale as a “True Volkswagen,” as the company calls it, bringing more than just a new name.
The ID. Tiguan is an upgrade in nearly every aspect over its predecessors, with a new design, updated tech, and refined interior.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Its “hallmark feature,” according to VW, is the completely redesigned exterior. Based on its new Pure Positive design language, the ID. Tiguan looks more like the gas-powered version with a traditional boxy SUV profile.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan (Source: Volkswagen)
Volkswagen’s new electric SUV trades the ID.4’s aerodynamic design for a wide, chunky front end. It also drops the flush door handles in favor of traditional pull-style handles.
As a result, the new ID. Tiguan “looks like a vehicle from the premium segment,” Volkswagen claimed.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan (Source: Volkswagen)
Inside, the ID. Tiguan features Volkswagen’s new interior design. The overhauled interior includes its new infotainment system, including a 10″ Digital Cockpit and 15″ center display screens. Plus, there’s an optional 12″ passenger screen.
One of the biggest changes inside is the return of physical buttons, which are now found below the center display and on the steering wheel.
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan interior (Source: Volkswagen)
There’s also a fun new “Retro” mode that transforms the Digital Cockpit with iconic blue-red instruments from the Golf IV.
Meanwhile, drivers can choose from six different classic VW models to display in a virtual “garage” on the infotainment screen: Golf I, Golf II Country, Golf IV, Tiguan I, Race Touareg, and Beetle.
The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:
a rear-wheel-drive version with 140 kW (190 PS) and a 58 kWh battery
a rear-wheel-drive version with 210 kW (286 PS) and a 77 kWh battery
and a 220 kW (299 PS) 4MOTION all-wheel-drive variant, also with a 77 kWh battery.
Depending on the battery size and configuration, the ID. Tiguan offers a WLTP range of up to 372 miles (600 km), a “new benchmark” for Volkswagen’s electric SUVs in Europe.
With up to 295 hp (299 PS), the ID. Tiguan can tow up to 4,400 lbs (2,000 kg) with the 77 kWh battery. With the 58 kWh battery, towing capacity is around 4,000 lbs (1,800 kg).
Volkswagen ID. Tiguan Digital Cockpit with Retro Mode (Source: Volkswagen)
The ID. Tiguan also comes with standard one-pedal driving and Volkswagen’s new Connected Travel Assist. It also supports vehicle-to-load (V2L), enabling it to power external electronics like an electric grill or e-bike.
For an added cost, buyers can upgrade to electronically adjustable front seats with memory and ventilation, a premium Harmon Kardon sound system, and a panoramic sunroof.
Volkswagen will launch the ID. Tiguan in Germany and several other European markets on October 13, with prices starting at 42,695 euros ($47,800). It will be available in four trims: Trend, Life, Style, and R-Line.
After it goes on sale in Europe through early 2027, Volkswagen said the ID. Tiguan will replace the ID.4 in North America.

They didn’t really improve the way it looks to me compared to the ID.4 it replaces. It actually has a more generic look. The lD.5 was the best looking in this category. The physical dials are definitely an improvement though.

“The Tiguan is our best-selling model worldwide, and the ID.4 and ID.5 are among our most successful electric cars,” VW Brand CEO Thomas Shafer said, adding that “The ID. Tiguan brings these two success stories together.”
Prices and other details will be announced “in due course,” the company said. The current VW ID.4 uses an 82 kWh battery that provides an EPA-estimated range of up to 291 miles in the RWD version. The AWD model offers around 263 miles.
Given the European model features nearly 25 miles (40 km) more WLTP range than the outgoing ID.4, the ID. Tiguan will likely offer over 300 miles on the EPA scale.
Volkswagen has not yet announced US prices. The outgoing ID.4 has a starting MSRP of around $45,000.

A U.S. Marine with 1st Reconnaissance Battalion, 1st Marine Division, fires a Switchblade 300 loitering munition system. The Switchblade 300 is the munition that will be incorporated into PERCH 2.0 (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Cpl. Jaye Townsend)
WASHINGTON — An updated version of General Dynamics Land Systems’ (GDLS) loitering munitions platform are set to be delivered to the Army by the end of the month, a company executive told Breaking Defense this week.
The platforms are the second iteration of the company’s Precision Effects & Reconnaissance-Canister-Housed , or PERCH system. The kit integrates on Abrams tanks and Stryker vehicles to provide beyond line-of-sight surveillance and is outfitted with AeroVironment’s (AV) Switchblade loitering munitions.
Four PERCH 2.0 prototypes will be delivered to Fort Hood’s 1st Brigade, 1st Cavalry Division by the end of October, where soldiers will integrate them into Abrams tanks for experiment ation, Scott Taylor, GDLS’ director of US growth, said.
The company developed the first PERCH iteration with internal research and development (IRAD) funding in response to reporting about the war in Ukraine, feedback from field commanders in Europe and discussions with senior leaders in III Armored Corps, Taylor said.
“So it’s sort of a rapid development, trying to meet the Army’s needs where they are,” he added.
After GDLS demonstrated its first PERCH iteration, which it debuted at last year’s AUSA, the Army provided feedback to GDLS. The company applied the Army’s comments to create the first prototype of PERCH 2.0, once again using IRAD funds.
Part of that initial feedback, Taylor explained, w as to incorporate enhanced beyond line-of-sight technology, make reloads easier, increase storage space — which the company did by switching out AV’s SB600 for the SB300 — and create a system that can fire without soldiers having to open hatches After evaluating the second version, Taylor said the Army found the design “compelling” and wanted a total of four prototypes. “We said, ‘Well, can you get some skin in the game?”’ Taylor recounted. The Army subsequently purchased three prototypes under the Abrams System Technical Support (STS) contract, which is updated periodically, with the PERCH 2.0 purchases added to the contract in August .
A spokesperson from GDLS later told Breaking Defense that “doing it that way allows us to move quickly to meet emerging needs.”
The Army has shown increased interest in mounting loitering munitions onto its armored vehicles. Apart from the Abrams tank, the service is looking to implement loitering munitions onto its replacement for the Bradley Infantry Vehicle, dubbed the XM30 .
As Breaking Defense previously reported , the two models the Army is currently choosing from — American Rheinmetall’s Lynx and GDLS’ Wolf — are both outfitted with options to attach loitering munitions. However, Taylor did not comment on what kinds of loitering munitions could be attached to the Wolf.

Kodiak AI and Charger Logistics have launched autonomous freight service on the 435-mile lane between Charger’s terminals in Dallas and Laredo, Texas, the companies announced Thursday. The trucks haul refrigerated and dry van freight for consumer packaged goods and food and beverage customers. The first delivery ran Sept. 8.
A safety driver is behind the wheel for now. The companies plan to move the lane to driverless operations once Kodiak completes its safety case.
Kodiak’s long-haul Autonomy Readiness Measure, which tracks the share of claims and evidence in that safety case, reached 96% at the end of Sept e mber . That was up from 93% at the end of August and 84% in February. The company plans to launch long-haul driverless service by the end of 2026 on its Dallas-Houston lane along Interstate 45 . Its driverless trucks have operated in commercial service in the Permian Basin since December 2024.
Refrigerated and dry van freight to Laredo
Laredo is the highest-volume commercial land port of entry in the U.S., and the Charger lane is Kodiak’s first route serving it. The Port of Laredo handled more than $350 billion in international trade in 2025, nearly 40% of all U.S. trade with Mexico, according to the Kodiak press release.
Consumer packaged goods and food and beverage freight moves in steady, high-volume flows tied to retail replenishment schedules, Kodiak said, which makes predictable transit times and longer operating hours worth more.
Charger is an asset-based carrier operating in the U.S. and Mexico, with temperature-controlled freight among its core service lines. It runs its network on a proprietary transportation management system and a set of in-house applications.
“Autonomy lets us build a network that serves both our customers and our drivers,” said Andy Khera, president of Charger Logistics, in the announcement. “Combining our in-house TMS, managed transportation, and the Kodiak Driver creates a nearly fully automated ecosystem that gives our customers long-term capacity continuity through changing labor markets and freight demand, while bringing our drivers home every night.”
Expansion into Charger’s fleet
Under its Driver-as-a-Service model, Kodiak deploys the Kodiak Driver on trucks its customers own and operate. The companies expect to add lanes in Charger’s network over time as the carrier integrates the Kodiak Driver into its own fleet.
Charger also has an autonomous trucking agreement with Aurora Innovation on the same lane. Aurora announced in late July that Charger would deploy Aurora’s second-generation driverless trucks between Dallas and Laredo. That deal, reported in August , is a transportation-as-a-service agreement, under which Aurora holds the U.S. Department of Transportation operating authority, controls the truck and carries the insurance.
“Charger came to us knowing what they wanted from autonomy and what they need to see before scaling it,” said Don Burnette, founder and CEO of Kodiak. “The Dallas–Laredo lane extends the Kodiak Driver into a new corridor, and gives both companies the operating foundation we need to scale driverless service.”

Pouring a gold bar. Credit: iStock
Posted By: Colin McClelland October 9, 2026
Gold miners are being urged to identify the refiners receiving metal from each operating mine under a World Gold Council disclosure framework aimed at making legitimate gold flows easier to distinguish from illicit trade.
Companies producing doré, the partly refined gold-and-silver bars poured at mine sites, should publish an annual list linking each mine to its refining partners and their countries, under the London-based council’s new disclosure guidance .
“It gives downstream partners, investors, regulators and other stakeholders more confidence in the integrity of the market while making it harder for opaque or irresponsible practices to hide in complexity,” council head of supply chain integrity Vivien Glass wrote in a commentary this week announcing the board’s adoption of the guidance.
The framework follows a September 2023 commitment by council members to disclose their refining partners. The latest step sets out a common reporting format, with exclusions for commercial and security information. It recommends disclosure across the doré-producing industry rather than establishing a legal reporting requirement.
Provenance concerns
The stakes were highlighted by New York Times investigations into Latin American gold entering North American supply chains. The Royal Canadian Mint pledged to expand sourcing disclosures in April after the newspaper found that some gold it refined may have come from Colombian cartel-controlled mines. The Mint said it had suspended refining material from the supply chain in question.
More recently, Venezuelan doré shipped to the U.S. under a Trafigura agreement with state-owned miner Minerven remained in storage because refiners were unwilling to handle it, the Times reported in September. Trafigura disputed the account on several points in comments to The Northern Miner .
Those cases underscore the distinction between identifying a metal’s source and establishing that it hasn’t financed criminal activity. The council’s framework would make mine-to-refiner relationships public, but the disclosures alone wouldn’t establish that gold was responsibly sourced.
Mine to refiner
The annual disclosure should identify each mine, its state and country, the refiner receiving its doré and the refiner’s country. Every recipient should be listed when a mine uses more than one refiner, the council said.
Members using toll processing should also disclose the mine-to-refiner relationship when they retain legal custody of the gold until export. Companies can include the information in annual or sustainability reports, or an equivalent publication.
The guidance recommends annual disclosure covering the preceding 12 months, but doesn’t specify the first reporting year or a publication deadline. A council spokesperson didn’t immediately reply to an email on Friday seeking clarification.
Shipment weights aren’t required. Transport companies, routes, traders and exporters can also remain undisclosed, along with other sensitive commercial details or information that could jeopardize workers’ safety.
The guidance excludes gold shipped as concentrate, carbon fines or low-grade sweepings. Those materials don’t typically go directly to a refinery, and naming their recipients could raise confidentiality or security concerns, the council said.
Earlier pledge
The council’s 2023 pledge covered 33 members with operating mines that collectively produced about 1,300 tonnes of gold annually. They committed to naming refining partners at least once a year for operations whose primary revenue came from gold production.
Members also pledged to join the Gold Bar Integrity platform and confidentially supply production data to refining partners. The new guidance doesn’t specify penalties for failing to disclose.
Pressure for broader transparency also extends to refiners. In a September 2025 submission on the London Bullion Market Association’s proposed disclosure changes, Human Rights Watch urged the association to require refiners to identify all mines of origin and suppliers, including those outside the council’s membership and suppliers of recycled gold.
Public supplier information can help affected communities, investors and other stakeholders respond when abuses occur, the rights group said.

Stord said Thursday it closed a $400 million credit facility led by Citi and hired new finance and revenue chiefs. The Atlanta-based fulfillment company said the facility closed oversubscribed at nearly double its original target.
Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, First Citizens, Citizens and KeyBank also participated. The deal follows a $250 million Series F led by Strike Capital in May that valued Stord at $3 billion. That brings Stord’s 2026 equity and credit capacity to $650 million, the company said.
“This facility, combined with our $250 million Series F, gives us the balance sheet to match the scale, potential, and impact of what we’re building,” said Sean Henry, CEO and co-founder of Stord, in the announcement. “We will use this capital to expand our fulfillment network, accelerate our deployment of robotics, and invest aggressively in AI through Stord Labs.”
The announcement did not disclose the facility’s structure, pricing or maturity.
Nearly 100 fulfillment locations
Revenue run-rate is approaching $1 billion, and the company has grown tenfold over the past four years, Stord said. Henry told Axios Pro the company has grown materially since its May raise. Stord, which is privately held, did not disclose revenue or profit figures.
The company says it runs nearly 100 fulfillment locations worldwide for more than 1,000 brands and processes more than $15 billion in gross merchandise volume a year. Its packages reach 1 in 4 U.S. households annually, according to Stord.
Acquisitions built part of that footprint: ProPack Logistics and Pitney Bowes’ e-commerce fulfillment unit in 2024, Ware2Go from UPS in May 2025 and Shipwire from Ceva Logistics in January. Ware2Go alone added 21 e-commerce warehouses with about 2.5 million square feet of storage capacity, and Shipwire brought 12 fulfillment centers.
Two hires from public companies
Bill Zerella, the new chief financial officer, has led finance at three public companies and took all three to the public markets, including Fitbit in its 2015 IPO. He most recently served as CFO of ACV Auctions.
Mark Wayland, the new chief revenue officer, was most recently chief revenue officer at Box and held the same title at Tanium before that. He spent more than a decade at Salesforce, where he rose to senior vice president of Marketing Cloud.
Both men come to Stord from NYSE-listed companies.
The new lenders and executives are “a vote of confidence in the foundation we’ve created at Stord, as well as a signal of where we are headed,” Henry said.

Tesla’s driver-assistance package is now called “Tesla Assisted Driving” in Europe. The company’s German website no longer mentions “Full Self-Driving,” and the old address now redirects to a new “Tesla Assisted Driving” page.
The rename follows Germany’s Transport Ministry calling the FSD name misleading, and it’s part of a deal that has Berlin backing Tesla’s push for EU-wide approval.
Germany wanted a new name, and Tesla offered one
In a statement published October 6 , Germany’s Federal Ministry of Transport (BMV) wrote that the name of the system formerly sold as “FSD – Full Self-Driving Supervised” is misleading because the system doesn’t take over the full driving task. The driver has to pay attention at all times and remains fully responsible for the car.
Tesla offered to rename it “Tesla Assisted Driving” during talks with Transport Minister Steffen Bilger in September, according to the ministry.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
They also agreed on speed. Germany says the system can go up to 10% over the speed limit, and it will back that position in the EU approval process. Tesla will need to change FSD to make that happen as it often goes way beyond 10% of the limit.
That’s a real concession from Tesla. Reuters reported that the version approved in the Netherlands allows speeds up to 50% over the detected limit.
In return, Bilger says he wants Tesla drivers to be able to use the system across the EU as quickly as possible. Musk thanked Germany on X with a “Danke schoen.”
Same pitch, new name
The rebrand is mostly a find-and-replace job. Not much else changed.
Tesla’s new German page is a translation of its US FSD page with the product name swapped out. It still says the car will drive you “almost anywhere” under your active supervision with minimal intervention. It still claims the system is “7x safer” than human drivers, a figure Tesla’s own footnote says is measured against the estimated US average. And it still ends with a section titled “Die Zukunft ist autonom” (“The future is autonomous”) that promotes Robotaxi and Cybercab.
Back in the US, tesla.com/fsd is still selling “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” for $99 a month.
Tesla’s page lists eight EU countries where the system is approved: the Netherlands, Lithuania, Estonia, Denmark, Belgium, Slovenia, Czechia and Croatia. Germany isn’t on the list yet. As we reported last month , the EU vote has slipped to December at the earliest, and bloc-wide approval needs 15 of 27 member states representing 65% of the EU population. France and Sweden have both raised concerns about speeding.
Electrek’s Take
This should be the name everywhere, and Tesla knows it.
“Full Self-Driving” was an aspiration when Tesla started selling it. In October 2016, Tesla said every car it was building had the hardware for full self-driving. At its Autonomy Day in April 2019, Musk said FSD would be “feature complete” by the end of that year and that Tesla would have over a million robotaxis on the road in 2020. You could argue the name was a bet on the future back then. A bad bet, but a bet.
Tesla has missed that target every single year since. It’s now been almost exactly 10 years since the 2016 announcement, and Tesla has admitted that the cars it sold as self-driving capable from 2016 to 2023 don’t have the hardware to do it. So at what point does an aspirational name become a false one? A California judge answered that last December , calling the name “unambiguously false and counterfactual.”

The peak shipping season for U.S. container imports is winding down after an unusually long stretch of elevated volumes through the summer and early fall, the National Retail Federation said.
The latest Global Port Tracker report, produced by NRF and Hackett Associates, indicates August was likely the busiest month of 2026, replacing September as the anticipated peak. Imports are expected to ease through the remainder of the year as retailers shift from stocking holiday merchandise to replenishing inventories and preparing for early 2027.
“Even with any fluctuations in final data, we’re likely past the busiest part of the year,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF’s vice president for supply chain and customs policy. “The truth is that the peak season started early and was stretched out through the summer and early fall, with the difference from month to month often amounting to little more than a rounding error.”
Ports covered by Global Port Tracker handled 2.3 million twenty-foot equivalent units in August, the latest month with finalized figures. That was up 0.4% from July but down 0.7% from August 2025.
The trade group lowered its September forecast to 2.28 million TEUs from the previously projected 2.31 million. The revised estimate would still represent an 8.2% increase from a year earlier. October imports are forecast at 2.25 million TEUs, up 8.5% year over year, before declining to 2 million TEUs in November.
Hackett Associates founder Ben Hackett said imports have been bolstered by robust consumer spending despite weakening economic indicators, declining consumer confidence and increasing inflation.
The projections point to a gradual retreat from summer highs rather than an abrupt drop in cargo demand. Despite the expected month-to-month slowdown, September and October volumes would remain above their year-earlier levels.
Gold said most holiday merchandise has already arrived, with “last-minute replenishment and preparation for early 2027” driving shipments for the balance of the year.
The retailers forecast full-year imports at the ports covered by the report at 25.8 million TEUs, up 1.4% from 2025.

Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO October 9, 2026
New drilling by Glencore (LSE: GLEN)-backed Hot Chili (ASX, TSX-V: HCH; US-OTC: HHLKF) has extended shallow copper-gold mineralization at its La Verde porphyry discovery in coastal Chile, strengthening the case for potential feed to the nearby Costa Fuego project.
Hole DKP075 lengthens a previously reported partial intersection to 188 metres grading 0.44% copper and 0.16 gram gold per tonne from 24 metres depth, Hot Chili said Thursday in a statement . It also intersected 29 metres grading 0.39% copper and 0.15 gram gold from 304 metres to the end of the hole.
With more than 35,000 metres of drilling already carried out at La Verde, Perth-based Hot Chili is aiming to complete an initial resource for the property by Dec. 31. Management’s goal is to use ore from La Verde to feed a planned processing plant for Costa Fuego – a copper-gold project about 30 km to the north — to cut costs. Both projects sit at low elevation in Chile’s Atacama region, about 600 km north of Santiago.
A coherent, higher-grade near-surface zone at La Verde could support low-strip-ratio open-pit mining during the early years of Costa Fuego’s 20-year mine plan, Hot Chili says.
Development plan
Hot Chili’s latest drill results “further speak to La Verde’s near (at) surface potential, which stands to significantly enhance Costa Fuego’s already robust 2025 prefeasibility study (PFS) mine plan with (higher-grade) ‘satellite’ feed,” ATB Cormark mining analyst Stefan Ioannou said Friday in a note.
Other drill highlights include hole DKP067, which cut 112 metres grading 0.40% copper and 0.10 gram gold from 42 metres downhole, including 26 metres of 0.59% copper and 0.14 gram gold from 62 metres.
Hole DKP078, meanwhile, intersected 240 metres grading 0.30% copper and 0.17 gram gold from 36 metres downhole. This included 54 metres grading 0.41% copper and 0.26 gram gold from 46 metres.
Assays from 25 drillholes remain pending.
Hot Chili plans to evaluate incorporating La Verde into a revised Costa Fuego PFS, which will be used to submit an Environmental Impact Assessment for the project in next year’s second quarter. This will initiate a roughly two-year approval process in support of a production start-up targeted for 2031.
Higher grade
Based on drilling to date, La Verde could potentially host more than 500 million tonnes of higher-grade satellite feed for Costa Fuego, Ioannou said in his note.
Costa Fuego hosts 502 million probable tonnes grading 0.37% copper, 0.1 gram gold, 0.49 gram silver and 97 parts per million molybdenum, according to a March 2025 reserve. Contained metal amounts to 1.86 million tonnes copper, 1.58 million oz. gold, 7.95 million oz. silver and 49,000 tonnes molybdenum.
Assuming an 8% discount rate, Costa Fuego has an after-tax net present value of $1.2 billion (C$1.7 billion), an internal rate of return of 19% and a payback period of 4.5 years, according to the 2025 PFS. Pre-production expenditures are estimated at $1.27 billion.
Copper production is estimated at 95,000 tonnes a year for the first 14 years.

Members from the Swedish air defense regiment participated in a handover ceremony in Halmstad, Sweden on November 18, 2021. (U.S. Army Photos by Sgt. 1st Class Terrance D. Rhodes)
STOCKHOLM — Against a backdrop of political controversy over Sweden’s approach to the nations on NATO’s eastern flank, Stockholm this week announced it will be sending Patriot batteries to Poland, the first time it has deployed the high-end air defenses as part of a NATO mission.
About 100 personnel from the Swedish Air Defense Regiment (Lv 6) in Halmstad will protect NATO’s logistics hub in southeastern Poland, outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said at a press briefing at the government headquarters on Tuesday. Saab Gripen fighters from the Blekinge Air Wing (F 17) are already flying over Poland this month to protect the same hub.
“All of this strengthens NATO, it strengthens Europe, and it strengthens Sweden,” said Kristersson.
The hub near the Ukrainian border is the main transit point for military and civilian aid to Ukraine under NATO’s Security Assistance and Training for Ukraine (NSATU). The Swedish unit will operate under NATO Air Command and contribute to NATO’s Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD).
Sweden is taking over the rotational role from the Netherlands, which has Patriot batteries there. The mandate runs from December with plans to continue into the first half of 2027, Defense Minister Pål Jonson said.
“We will also gain important operational and strategic experience with a very close ally, as Poland is. These are rotational deployments to which we are now contributing in solidarity,” Jonson said.
Jonson stressed that the security situation in Sweden’s immediate neighborhood “is very serious,” citing intensified hybrid operations against Europe. “Moscow’s purpose is clear,” he said. “It is about trying to undermine support for Ukraine. It is about trying to intimidate our societies and create division and fear. Russia will not succeed in that.”
He concluded that Sweden “must prepare for a deteriorated security situation in the neighborhood for a prolonged period,” and pointed to several recent cases. Alongside the incident at Germany’s Leipzig Airport in August, the Estonian recently security service claimed that Russian intelligence services were behind the August attack on the defense company Milrem in Tallinn.
In Sweden, the current cabinet is a caretaker government after September’s parliamentary election, in which the red-green-center bloc won by a narrow margin. However, no government has been formed, and it is unclear when the parties will cohere around a new leader.
As a result, Kristersson, who has been prime minister since October 2022 with the conservative Moderate Party, is acting as a caretaker at a time when the security situation is shaky.
“Almost every day something happens that affects security in Sweden and Europe. We are monitoring it constantly. We are on our toes. Our authorities are on their toes,” he said.
The caretaker government is, as he noted, quite limited when it comes to new domestic-policy initiatives. However, Kristersson said, it “is not limited when it comes to protecting Sweden — that is, Swedish interests, Sweden’s security, and the security of Swedes in Sweden or abroad. That is also important to say.”
Foreign Minister Questions PM Candidate Andersson
Underlining Kristersson’s point that the security situation does not pause while Sweden works out its politics, an internal row broke out this week between the rival parties.
Social Democratic leader and prime-ministerial candidate Magdalena Andersson told Politico on election day that the outgoing government had focused too narrowly on the Baltic region and ignored “the global south,” seemingly an indication that should Andersson manage to form a government, Sweden’s focus on NATO’s eastern flank could change.
Andersson is in a second round of talks after the Speaker of the Riksdag again tasked her with forming a government that parliament can tolerate. She first received the mandate, returned it, and has now been given it again.
Politico’s story was later updated to say that Andersson’s office clarified she was not criticizing efforts to strengthen work in the Baltic region, but opponents, including the caretaker government, have tried to jump on her comments as a sign that a Social Democrat-led coalition will be less committed to defending NATO’s eastern flank.
Speaking to Breaking Defense on the sideline of Tuesday’s briefing, outgoing Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard painted Andersson’s comments in a negative light, saying “I actually think it gives the impression that one does not really have a grasp of the situation, and that is very concerning because she [Andersson] aspires to become prime minister in a historically difficult period for security policy.”
Malmer Stenergard added that “I want a prime minister who is comfortable with the security issues,” and ” who does not make sweeping statements about nuclear weapons without actually having grounds for them, and “who truly prioritizes security in the immediate neighborhood, because that is how we build security for Sweden.”
The day after Malmer’s Stenergard’s comments, Andersson posted on X , saying, “A government I lead will be a strong, reliable and active ally in NATO. In turbulent times, we are stronger together.”

Nearly half of manufacturing HR professionals say they struggle with job candidates using AI to misrepresent themselves, according to Criteria’s 2026–2027 Hiring Benchmark Report . At the same time, more than two-thirds are using AI in their own recruiting or hiring processes.
What’s Related
The survey found that 45% of manufacturing respondents identified AI misrepresentation as a hiring challenge, compared with 41% across all industries. Manufacturing ranked behind technology (60%) and professional services (47%).
Criteria surveyed 1,027 U.S. hiring professionals in summer 2026. Manufacturing accounted for 11% of respondents, whose roles included human resources, hiring management, and business ownership.
The findings describe a hiring process in which AI is becoming common on both sides of the application. Employers use it to evaluate candidates, while many say applicants use it to present an inaccurate picture of themselves.
RELATED STORIES: Gartner Warns AI-Driven Hiring Freeze Could Backfire by 2030 | New Study Says AI Helps Workers and Creates More Warehouse Roles
Employers unsure what to believe
Across all industries, 24% of respondents said they had lost confidence in résumés as a reliable way to judge candidates. Another 35% said their current hiring process could not reliably detect when candidates used AI to misrepresent themselves.
These findings cover all industries surveyed. They show employers’ concerns, but don’t tell us how many applicants actually misled them.
Finding qualified candidates remains the larger challenge. Among manufacturing respondents, 47% reported persistent skills shortages, and 53% said hiring was more difficult than a year earlier.
Despite those difficulties, 74% of manufacturing respondents expected to hire more in the coming year. That was higher than the 64% reported across all industries.
Manufacturers also using AI to hire
Manufacturing had the second-highest reported use of AI in recruiting or hiring, at 69%, behind technology’s 87%. Across the full survey, 56% said they used AI in those processes.
The report found AI being used for tasks ranging from screening applications to scheduling and interviews. Across all respondents, 46% reported using AI for screening, while 35% used it for assessments and 35% for scheduling.
Employers also identified obstacles to using the technology themselves. Accuracy was the most common concern, cited by 42% of respondents, followed by data privacy at 33%.
Even with those concerns, 72% of manufacturing respondents were optimistic about AI’s role in improving hiring, and 64% were confident it would improve the quality of their hiring decisions.

AI
Workstation
GMKtec-EVO-X3-AI-Mini-PC-Hero
Calling AMD’s Ryzen AI Max+ chips well-received in the mini-PC market is probably an understatement. The high-performance Zen 5 chips have proven particularly adept in this market thanks to a combination of CPU and iGPU performance, plus high memory capacity and bandwidth from LPDDR5X. Especially in this era of AI development, software developers looking to test and run inference locally have been quick to snap up the mini-PCs.
One result of this popularity is that AMD’s many mini-PC partners have been addressing a market large enough (and with margins big enough) to justify working through multiple generations of mini-PC designs within the Ryzen AI Max family’s lifecycle. A prime example is GMtec, one of the industry’s better-known mini-PC vendors. Last year the company released its first Ryzen AI Max+ box with the EVO-X2 , and this year they are back again with a new and very different Ryzen AI Max+ mini-PC design that they are dubbing the EVO-X3.
GMKtec EVO-X3 Key Specs (As Configured)
Processors | AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, 16C/32T (5.1GHz)
Operating System | Windows 11 Pro
Memory | 128GB LPDDR5X-8000, Soldered
Drive Bays | 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Lexar NQ790 4TB) 1x M.2 2280 PCIe Gen4 x4 (Empty)
GPU | Radeon 8060S Graphics (40 CUs)
PSU | 230W External PSU
Form Factor | Mini-PC
Dimensions | 353 x 186 x 41 mm (13.9 x 7.3 x 1.6 in)
Weight | 2.3kg (5.07 lbs)
Wireless | Wi-Fi 7 (2×2) + Bluetooth 5.4 (MT7925)
Color | Gray & Neon Green
Ports | Front: 1x USB-A 5Gbps, 1x USB-A 480Mbps, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack Rear: 2x HDMI 2.1, 1x USB-C 40Gbps, 1x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x 2.5GbE LAN (RJ45, RTL8125BG), 1x OCuLink (Gen4 x4)
The EVO-X3 stands out in a crowded mini-PC market for a few reasons. First and foremost, the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 SoC at the heart of the system delivers its AI performance and enables it to tap into 128GB of LPDDR5X memory for its iGPU. The second, and far more unique reason is its connectivity. GMKtec has outfitted the system with an OCuLink port, making it a rare Ryzen AI Max system with external PCIe connectivity, and it surpasses even Thunderbolt 4 systems in available bandwidth.
Surprisingly, GMKtec is aiming the EVO-X3 at a pretty broad customer base, even pitching the OCuLink port as a gaming feature for use with an eGPU. In practice, though, it is hard to imagine the system being used as anything other than a productivity desktop, especially since GMKtec even preloads the system with AI development software. That is okay, because the Ryzen AI Max platform has proven well suited for that role.
If you wanted to find the GMKtec EVO-X3 online, here is an Amazon Affiliate link .
GMKtec EVO-X3 External hardware Overview
One of the most notable design aspects of the previous iteration, the EVO-X2 mini-PC, was that the system operates upright, a pretty big distinction from the more classic wide-and-low desktop mini-PC form factors. For the EVO-X3, GMKtec seems to have doubled down on this design strategy even more, resulting in a mini-PC that can only be described as a metal monolith. The stange form factor makes more sense once we get inside.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Front Angled 3
The metal, by the way, is a notable change from the EVO-X2, which notably (and noticeably) featured a plastic chassis. On the other hand, this EVO-X3 is fully metal. The overall monolithic design is even more clearly meant to stand, especially with the (required) base attached.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Front 1
The tall, slim profile does mean that there is very little to the front of the system, though. For the purposes of our article layout (and your browser window), we have laid the mini-PC flat, which goes to show just how thin the 41mm PC is. Despite packing in a high-performance processor, it is not much thicker than a desktop replacement-class workstation laptop.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-USB 3.2 Type-A Port 1
This view also underscores the limited I/O connectivity on the front of the PC, however. Aside from the 3.5mm combo audio jack, GMKtec has placed only two USB-A ports on the front of the system, and only one is a fast 5Gbps USB 3.x port. The second USB-A port is an even slower USB 2.x port, and there is no front-panel USB Type-C connectivity. The system supports plenty of I/O bandwidth, as we will see, but just not in the front.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Power Button 1
Meanwhile, towards the other end of the system, we find a rather striking neon green power button sitting within the grey metal chassis.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Side 4
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Side 3
Speaking of aesthetics, the EVO-X3’s standing design is not just a style choice for GMKtec. Both the left and right sizes feature significant ventilation. Meanwhile, if there is any doubt about what the primary market is for this system, the “AI workstation” labeling etched into the left side of the case should remove all doubt.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Rear 1
Shifting to the rear of the system, we find much better ventilation with clearly visible heatsinks. More importantly, this is also where the rest of the system’s I/O lives, including its unusual OCuLink port.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-OCuLink Port 1
Starting there, GMKtec has opted to route four of the Ryzen SoC’s PCIe lanes to an OCuLink port for directly attaching a device to the system. This port can technically connect any device, but the most common use for OCuLink these days is attaching a dock for an external GPU, making it possible to add a high-end video card (or other accelerator) to the system. The OCuLink specification itself tops out at PCIe Gen4 x4 (or ~64Gbps), so it is not comparable to the amount of bandwidth a full-fledged PCIe slot can offer. With the Ryzen AI Max chips offering only 16 PCIe lanes to begin with (all PCIe Gen4), GMKtec can realistically offer only 4 lanes, since they need the other lanes for other features.
In any case, the drawback to OCuLink as an external port is the same here as it always was: it is not a hot-plug-capable port. That is why GMKtec has put a very explicit sticker here warning users not to plug (or unplug) an OCuLink cable while the system is operating. On that note, credit to the engineer who had the foresight here to put the OCuLink port to the left of the DC power jack, isolating it from the hotplug-capable USB ports.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-DC Power Input 2
The thin profile of the EVO-X3 means that GMKtec is relying on an external power supply here. At 230 Watts, they technically could have gotten away with a USB-C power supply, but barrel jack units are still a common fixture here.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-HDMI 2.1 Port 1
Next is the system’s sole USB-C port. A native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, this is a full 40Gbps USB4 port that also supports DP Alt Mode to double as a display output for the system. In fact, this is the only way to get DisplayPort video out of the X3, as there is also no dedicated DisplayPort output on the system. Otherwise, given GMKtec’s focus on external I/O bandwidth with the X3, it is somewhat surprising to see that they did not include a second 40Gbps USB-C port, as the Ryzen SoC provides for two ports.
To the right, we have the system’s sole dedicated display output: an HDMI 2.1 port. Another native feature of the Ryzen AI Max SoC, there is little reason not to include it here.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-USB 3.2 Type-A Port 4
Moving down the line, we find another USB Type-A port. The second (and final) USB port on the rear of the system is a 10Gbps port. Including the earlier Type-C port, this gives the X3 a total of 4 USB ports, which is serviceable, but it falls short compared to most other Ryzen AI Max mini-PCs that offer a few more ports. In practice, it means the OCuLink port and USB-C port are doing a lot of heavy lifting as far as I/O goes, as there simply are not a lot of ports otherwise for plugging in peripherals after you add a mouse and keyboard. There is again a reason for this that we will see inside.
Finally, we have the system’s dedicated Ethernet jack. This is a 2.5GbE port backed by Realtek’s RTL8125BG controller. This is a common enough sight across PCs these days, but for a recently-released Ryzen AI Max system, it is a shame that GMKtec did not use one of Realtek’s newer 10GbE chips, which have become readily available (and relatively cheap) this year. Not including 10GbE is quickly becoming a missed opportunity for AI development-focused PC.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Rear Angled 1
Shifting perspectives once again, here is a shot of what is on top of the X3 when the system is standing. Matching the colorful neon green accent of the power button we saw earlier, the solid green top gives the system a distinct two-tone color scheme. And perhaps a smidge of irony for the Ryzen-powered system, since it is much closer to NVIDIA’s shade of green than AMD’s.
In any case, the top features another airflow vent as well. So, like virtually every other side of the system, it needs to be kept clear for cooling purposes. This also serves as the one significant non-metallic portion of the system for cleanly routing the wireless radio antennas.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Bottom 1
Last but not least, here is a look at the bottom of the system. Normally hidden by the system’s base, this is where GMKtec has placed the product stickers, as well as the means to access the system’s internals.
GMKtec EVO-X3 AI Mini PC-Base Kit 2
Looking at the base itself, interestingly, GMKtec has opted to etch the full system information into the base, including its power specifications and regulatory trademarks. This ensures that the information is visible without dismantling the system, but it means that the base is an integral part of the system for more than just holding up the monolithic mini-PC.
The base relies on a pair of screws to secure it to the bottom of the mini-PC’s chassis. GMKtec has also taken care to include rubber feet on the base to prevent slippage. Unfortunately, these feet are not built into the base, and in fact have to be removed to access the screws that hold the base on. Which means this is not a design that is meant to be opened more than a couple of times, as it will wear out the adhesive on the feet.
Now that we have taken a look at the outside of the EVO-X3, let us dig into the guts of the system.

Inside Sion Power's advanced lithium-metal production facility. (Image courtesy of Sion Power.)
The US military is asking more of its unmanned systems, all of which are constrained by the energy capacity of today’s batteries. The demand for increasingly capable and power-hungry drones means the battery’s capability determines range, endurance, payload, and time on station.
Breaking Defense spoke with Sion Power CTO Job Rijssenbeek about advances in high-capacity battery chemistry, where lithium-metal technology may be applicable, and why batteries and unmanned platforms increasingly need to be co-designed as a single system.
Breaking Defense: As unmanned systems take on more demanding missions, is energy becoming a limiting factor in what they can do?
Job Rijssenbeek is chief technology officer of Sion Power.
Rijssenbeek : Absolutely. Brig. Gen. Troy Denomy, program acquisition executive for maneuver, summed up energy challenges at GVSETS (Ground Vehicle Systems Engineering & Technology Symposium) this past summer when he said, ‘Every formation we have today is underpowered.’ The insatiable demand for energy will only increase.
For airborne platforms, every pound matters. More weight requires more energy to lift, which requires more batteries, which add more weight. This quickly becomes a vicious circle. If you can put more energy into the same battery weight, you meaningfully change that math. Greater energy density batteries become enablers of greater range, endurance, and mission capability. They put more missions within reach.
What has changed in battery technology to make improvements in power, weight, and performance possible?
Lithium-ion technology has been extraordinarily successful, and will remain the right choice for many applications, but it is reaching its entitlement performance. There are several advanced battery chemistries coming onto the market, but there isn’t one chemistry that’s best for every mission. The different chemistries and ways of putting those together deliver different combinations of energy, power, cycle life, safety, and cost.
For applications where weight and endurance are especially important, lithium-metal anode batteries are compelling because replacing the graphite anode with lithium metal reduces weight and volume, and increases energy density. Those gains significantly enhance mission capability.
Sion Power has been at the forefront of lithium-metal battery innovation for more than 25 years. Over the last 15 years, we’ve developed robust IP around high-energy density batteries for electric vehicles. In the process, we developed lithium anode production technology, electrolyte formulations, cell designs, and packaging that makes this promising chemistry practical and applicable for aerospace and defense applications.
Today we’re producing large-format lithium-metal cells in Tucson, Arizona that offer double the energy density of conventional lithium-ion batteries, at the cell and pack level, which is transformational for drones and the missions they can fulfill.
What does higher energy density mean in practical terms for defense customers?
More energy at the same or lower weight translates into extended mission duration or additional payload. You can fly longer, reach farther, and do more.
Our maximum energy, one-way attack Licerion Strike cell is designed to deliver up to 500 Wh/kg at the cell level, compared with roughly 250 Wh/kg for today’s standard lithium-ion drone batteries. This means roughly twice the flight time, which translates to greater reach, significantly greater time on station, and enhanced effectiveness. For example, drones are being asked to carry increasingly greater electronic payloads (like communications, jamming, autonomous guidance, etc.), which consume hundreds of watts of continuous power. Higher-energy batteries allow operators to incorporate more of these capabilities without sacrificing endurance.
Defense systems must operate safely and reliably in harsh environments. How do lithium-metal cells perform under abuse conditions and temperature extremes?
Higher energy density is a benefit only if the cell can operate reliably under the conditions the mission requires. Any time more energy goes into a smaller package, safety always has to be front of mind. I’m proud to say that safety has always been our top priority at Sion Power. We design for safety rigorously, from the materials to the battery pack.
At our Tucson facility, we have approximately 2,000 test channels and a 5,300-square-foot safety and abuse lab dedicated to rigorous performance and safety testing – from exposure to extreme temperatures and vibration, to nail penetration, and forced discharge.
We understand that our batteries need to perform reliably in diverse environments and conditions, and we are constantly expanding the capabilities on that front.
Licerion Strike demonstration pack on commercial drone. (Image courtesy of Sion Power.)
What happens when you take lithium-metal batteries out of the lab and put them onto an actual drone?
We asked ourselves the same question earlier this year, as we shifted our application focus to drones. To find out, we fitted one of our Licerion Strike demonstration packs onto a commercially available Freefly Astro Max drone, replacing the drone’s two conventional lithium-ion batteries. Our pack increased onboard energy by over 50 percent and reduced the pack weight by nearly 30 percent, all while using the same mechanical footprint.
More importantly, the drone flew nearly twice as long when equipped with our battery, increasing from 33 minutes to 60 minutes.
Twice the flight time means reaching targets twice as far away and putting the pilot further out of harm’s way. Twice the flight time also means more time to be productive at the target. For example, if the target area is 15 minutes away, a 33-minute aircraft has only about three minutes on station before it must return. That’s not a lot of time to be effective. However, at 60 minutes of endurance, that enables 30 minutes on station. Imagine what more you can do in 30 minutes that you cannot do in 3 minutes. That’s the kind of difference operators care about.
Can lithium-metal technology be manufactured at defense-relevant scale and cost?
Absolutely. We’re shipping cells today from Tucson and are ramping 10–20 MWh of pilot-line capacity. We have plans for expanding to 100–200 MWh and more as demand increases. While we replace graphite with a lithium metal anode, all the other battery components are the same as those used in commercialized lithium-ion batteries. We already tap those supply chains to minimize our cell costs. As our manufacturing scale increases, our cost position will improve further.
Which drones would benefit most from lithium-metal, and where else could higher energy density change the performance equation?
Our lithium-metal solutions are ideal for heavier Group 1 and Group 2 drones where the range and payload benefits are significant. Group 3 drones tend to be powered by internal combustion engines today but will benefit from greater electrification and noise reduction that high-energy batteries will enable. Beyond drones, we anticipate our cells will be able to support robotics, automotive, and space applications in the future. If weight and energy are constraints, our batteries will help.
Licerion Strike lithium-metal cell. (Image courtesy of Sion Power.)
Is lithium-metal technology primarily suited to one-way applications, or can the technology also support rechargeable systems?
Lithium-metal batteries are absolutely rechargeable. Our work for automotive was foundational to demonstrating this.
We developed large-format 400 Wh/kg Licerion pouch cells that achieve 800 charge-discharge cycles, are fast-charge capable, and were validated by leading global OEMs. While our Licerion Strike product is aimed at maximum energy density, we’ve applied those learnings to Licerion Echo, our rechargeable solution, which is designed to deliver high energy density with over 150 cycles. Rechargeability increases flexibility, supports reuse, and reduces replacement demand.
China dominates the global supply chain for battery-grade materials. How can battery technologies reduce that dependency?
China’s supply chain dominance was established over decades and that will not be undone overnight. There isn’t a single chemistry that eliminates every supply-chain vulnerability.
One advantage of lithium-metal batteries is that the anode doesn’t require graphite, which removes one key dependence from the bill of materials.
I’m proud to say that Sion Power’s batteries are 100 percent manufactured in the United States. We already have a low dependence on China-made materials, and we are systematically qualifying alternative material sources to strengthen our supply chain resilience and comply with US defense sourcing requirements.
What needs to change in how batteries and unmanned systems are designed to unlock the next leap in capability?
I don’t think drone dominance will be based on one particular chemistry; rather, it’s about using the right chemistry for the mission.
For drones where endurance and weight are critical, lithium-metal represents a significant step forward in energy density. But the bigger change will come when batteries and unmanned systems are increasingly co-designed. That will enable greater optimization of range, payload, power, cycle life, and cost at the system level. The real acceleration comes when we stop optimizing the drone and the battery separately and start optimizing the entire system as one. That kind of approach turns improvements into capabilities that deliver decisive advantages today and create new opportunities for the future.

By: Staff Writer October 9, 2026
Expanding Canada’s mining tax incentives could attract up to $1.6 billion (US$1.1 billion) in additional annual exploration spending, accounting firm EY estimated in an analysis commissioned by the B.C.-based Association for Mineral Exploration (AME).
Including feasibility work in eligible exploration expenses and extending tax credits could help advance three to five additional mines under favourable market and policy conditions, according to EY’s economic assessment .
“Canada has what the world needs, and we have the opportunity to secure the mineral supply chain, strengthen Canada’s military capacity and ensure Canada’s long-term national and industrial sovereignty,” AME president and CEO Todd Stone said in an Oct. 7 statement .
The association wants engineering, feasibility and technical costs included under Canadian exploration expenses, a category of deductions companies can transfer to investors through flow-through shares. The push targets a financing gap between discovering a deposit and establishing whether it can support a mine.
Budget hurdle
The Liberal Party’s election platform pledged to expand eligible exploration activities. But Budget 2025 proposed explicitly excluding expenses incurred to determine a mineral resource’s economic viability or engineering feasibility from Canadian exploration expenses.
That proposal followed a British Columbia Supreme Court decision allowing a broader interpretation of the provincial equivalent of the deduction. Technical studies have generally been excluded under the Canada Revenue Agency’s interpretation of the federal rules, according to the budget documents .
AME is seeking broader eligibility in Budget 2026, building on its earlier appeal to Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne.
Budget 2025 separately proposed adding 12 minerals to the 30% Critical Mineral Exploration Tax Credit. That incentive is distinct from the 15% Mineral Exploration Tax Credit.
Conditional gains
The upper estimates assume tax changes alongside strong commodity prices, better permitting, infrastructure investment and improved access to capital. They aren’t guaranteed outcomes from expanding expense eligibility alone.
Higher exploration spending could add $5.2 billion to $12.2 billion to gross domestic product over 2026–2035, EY estimated. The associated employment benefit is 14,000 to 34,000 years of full-time employment over that decade, rather than that many permanent jobs.
Three to five additional mines could contribute another $12.9 billion to $21.4 billion to GDP over construction and 15 to 20 years of operations. AME’s headline figure of up to $33 billion therefore combines benefits over different periods.
Expanded incentives could cost $6.6 billion in forgone tax revenue over 10 years, EY estimated. Its five-to-one comparison measures GDP generated against that fiscal cost, rather than money returned to government.
British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia and Yukon support expanding eligible expenses, AME said.
“Right now, there is not a single public policy that the premiers are more united on that would have such a significant impact on investment here in Canada,” Stone said.

source_document.body:
The executive order (EO) from President Donald Trump on implementing the red dye diesel tax break has been formally published, but it is thin on fixing a fundamental problem with the policy: state and federal rules are not in sync.
The executive order was published in the Federal Register Friday. It is just four pages in length.
After citing unspecified “historic efforts to ensure fuel affordability for our citizens,” the executive order says “it is clear that further temporary relief is necessary.”
The EO directs Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent to “use his authority to defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations.” Bessent also is to look at waiving penalties that might other be incurred for the use of red dye diesel in over the road applications.
Red dye diesel gets its name through the fact that it is red in appearance because a dye has been blended into it. The dye has no impact on its performance.
The dye is blended so that certain end uses, primarily agricultural, can consume red dye diesel and avoid paying the federal excise taxes of 24.3 cts/g. Federal excise taxes on diesel also include a 0.1 cts/g fee for the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund Fee.
Break goes through December 31
The deferral period, if it is declared following a five-day review period, would be for October 5 through the end of the year.
But the goal is that the deferral be made permanent, so that the tax break for the remainder of the year ultimately would not need to be paid.
“The Secretary shall explore avenues, including legislation, to eliminate the obligation to pay the amounts deferred pursuant to the Secretary’s exercise of authority described in section 2 of this order,” the EO said.
But states have laws that prevent the consumption of red dye diesel on their respective roads. Wholesale and retail outlets are set up to provide a supply chain for non-dyed diesel which remains liable for the federal excise taxes, and that means they in only rare cases would have segregated tanks and pipelines that are targeted at red dye diesel.
The EO calls on the Treasury Secretary to “engage with State governments, relevant industry leadership as determined by the Administrator, and relevant labor organizations as determined by the Administrator to encourage safe and expedient coordination between the Federal Government and these various stakeholders in furtherance of the policies of this order.”
Some states already have acted
A wide range of states have changed their policies in recent weeks to allow red dye diesel on their roads. Texas, Indiana, Illinois, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, North Carolina, Arkansas and Alabama are all states that have made some sort of concession in their state rules to promote the use of red dye diesel and its lower cost.
But as has been noted by several critics of the red dye diesel policy, crossing from a state with a waiver into one that doesn’t have it is going to create a tax-paying nightmare for trucking companies. The extra bookkeeping effort may not be worth the tax break.
As Breakthrough Fuel said in a summary of the proposed change, after rating the impact from the tax shifts to be “low” at the retail level, it noted that “Highway lanes rarely carry dyed fuel, interstate routes cross non-relief states, and clear diesel pricing is unchanged by the order.”
The order also targets greater distribution by ordering the Treasury Secretary to “(coordinate) with agricultural cooperatives, rural fuel distributors, farm supply organizations, and other agricultural stakeholders, as determined by the Secretary of Agriculture, to ensure adequate distribution of dyed diesel for their use in high-demand areas.”
